notes.w: The cycle of think, call a tool, read the result.
notes.lead: The Agent SDK lets you embed Claude Code's autonomous agent loop in your own applications.
pts: How the agent loop works
The SDK is a standalone package that gives you programmatic control over tools, permissions, cost limits, and output.
Both the TypeScript and Python SDKs bundle a native Claude Code binary, so most installs need no separate Claude Code install.
Turns and messages
Turn 3: Claude calls Edit to fix auth.ts, then calls Bash to re-run npm test.
For example, max_turns=2 in the loop above would have stopped before the edit step.
Parallel tool execution
Read-only tools (like Read, Glob, Grep, and MCP tools marked as read-only) can run concurrently.
Tools that modify state (like Edit, Write, and Bash) run sequentially to avoid conflicts.
Turns and budget
When either limit is hit, the SDK returns a ResultMessage with a corresponding error subtype (error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd).
Once spend reaches the cap, spawning another subagent fails with Budget limit reached, and Claude Code stops any background subagents still running.
Permission mode
Tools pre-approved by permission rules run, and so do calls that need no approval in default mode, such as file reads inside your working directories.
In the TypeScript SDK, also requires allowDangerouslySkipPermissions: true in options.
Keep context efficient
Be selective with tools. Every tool definition takes context space. Use the tools field on AgentDefinition to scope subagents to the minimum set they need.
Use lower effort for routine tasks. Set effort to "low" for agents that only need to read files or list directories. This reduces token usage and cost.
Put it all together
Because a single-shot query() call raises after yielding an error result, the loop is wrapped in a try block so the script exits cleanly when a limit is hit.
When the agent finishes successfully, the example prints a Done: line with the agent's summary of the fix, then a line like Cost: $0.0312.

notes.w: Know what each run cost.
notes.lead: The Claude Agent SDK provides detailed token usage information for each interaction with Claude.
pts: Understand token usage

TypeScript provides per-step token breakdowns on each assistant message (message.message.id, message.message.usage), per-model cost via modelUsage on the result message, and a cumulative total on the result message.

Python provides per-step token breakdowns on each assistant message as message.usage and message.message_id, per-model cost via model_usage on the result message, and the cumulative total on the result message as total_cost_usd.
Track costs in streaming input mode
usage: covers only that turn, and within it only the main agent loop, not any subagents it ran.
The /clear turn's own result: covers only what has run since the reset, and carries a new session_id.
Track per-step usage
Track which IDs you've already counted and skip duplicates to avoid inflated totals.
Per-step output_tokens is a placeholder, so read output tokens from the result message.
Read output tokens from the result message

Claude Code builds each assistant message from the usage the API reported when the response began, so the message's output_tokens is only the count the API had reported at message_start, before the response was generated.
Read output tokens from the result's usage, or from modelUsage for a per-model breakdown.
Recover totals after a session crash
Step 1 recovers the full totals whenever an earlier result exists; the fallback in step 2 recovers only the main loop's input and cache tokens.

Go to step 2 instead when that result can't help you: * The call was single-shot, so no earlier result exists. * The crash happened on the first turn. * The turn before the crash was the /clear itself, so its result covers only the reset.
Track cache tokens
cache_creation_input_tokens: tokens used to create new cache entries (charged at a higher rate than standard input tokens).
In Python, they appear as keys in the ResultMessage.usage dict (for example, message.usage.get("cache_read_input_tokens", 0)).
Extend the prompt cache TTL to one hour

Cache entries for your own turns use a 5-minute TTL by default when you authenticate with an API key or run on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, or Claude Platform on AWS.

If your workload runs many short sessions against the same system prompt and context with gaps longer than 5 minutes between them, the cache expires between sessions and each new session pays full input price.

notes.w: Add the one tool your agent needs.
notes.lead: Custom tools extend the Agent SDK by letting you define your own functions that Claude can call during a conversation.
pts: Give Claude custom tools
Using the SDK's in-process MCP server, you can give Claude access to databases, external APIs, domain-specific logic, or any other capability your application needs.
Add more tools
A server holds as many tools as you list in its tools array.
Tool search is on by default and defers SDK MCP tools: Claude sees each tool's name in a compact list and loads its full schema on demand.
Require approval for specific tools
Set a tool's permission_policy to always_ask, and allowedTools stops approving that tool's calls, so they can reach your canUseTool callback even though the tool is listed.
Set the hint explicitly, because an unset destructiveHint counts as false for always_ask calls rather than defaulting to true.
Handle errors
A non-200 HTTP status is caught from the response and returned as an error result.
A network error or invalid JSON is caught by the surrounding try/except (Python) or try/catch (TypeScript) and also returned as an error result.
Images
An image block carries the image bytes inline, encoded as base64.
To return an image that lives at a URL, fetch it in the handler, read the response bytes, and base64-encode them before returning.
Return structured data
Use it to return raw values that Claude can read as exact fields instead of parsing them out of a text string or image.
To return structuredContent from Python, run a standalone MCP server instead of an in-process SDK server.
Example: unit converter
A user can ask "convert 100 kilometers to miles" or "what is 72°F in Celsius," and Claude picks the right unit type and units from the request.
Because tool search is on by default, the output may also include a ToolSearch call as Claude loads the deferred tool schema.

notes.t: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks
notes.w: Log every tool call, or block one.
notes.lead: Hooks are callback functions that run your code in response to agent events, like a tool being called, a session starting, or execution stopping.
pts: Asynchronous output
By default, the agent waits for your hook to return before proceeding.
If your hook performs a side effect, such as logging or sending a webhook, and doesn't need to influence the agent's behavior, you can return an async output instead.
Block the action when a callback fails
To block the action instead, set onFailure: "block" in TypeScript or on_failure="block" in Python on the matcher.
The tool result includes failed; blocking because onFailure is "block", and Claude doesn't see your error text.
Startup errors for onFailure
Claude Code doesn't support the option: the error includes does not honor. Update Claude Code, or remove the option.
The session was already running and didn't register your hooks: the error includes did not register your hooks. Start a new session.
Hook not firing
Ensure the hook is under the correct event type in options.hooks
Hooks may not fire when the agent hits the max_turns limit because the session ends before hooks can execute
Hook timeout
When you don't set one, Claude Code uses the event's default: 600 seconds for most events, 30 seconds for UserPromptSubmit, PreModelSwitch, and PostModelSwitch, and 10 seconds for MessageDisplay.
Claude Code runs SessionEnd callbacks during shutdown under the shorter SessionEnd timeout budget, 1.5 seconds by default.
Session hooks not available in Python
SessionStart and SessionEnd can be registered as SDK callback hooks in TypeScript, but aren't available in the Python SDK because its HookEvent type omits them.
In Python, they are only available as shell command hooks defined in settings files such as .claude/settings.json.
systemMessage not appearing in output
To pass context to the model instead, return additionalContext.
For any other event, the output appeared only in the lifecycle events that includeHookEvents (include_hook_events in Python) adds.

pts: Ephemeral sessions
The script prints each message as it arrives, including a result message whose subtype is success when the task completes within the turn limit.

If the task hits the 20-turn limit instead, the result message's subtype is error_max_turns and the query() call raises an error after yielding it, so wrap the loop in a try block if the container needs to exit cleanly.
Multi-agent container
Best for agents that must collaborate closely, for example multi-agent simulations where the agents interact with each other in a shared environment.
Give each agent its own working directory so they do not overwrite each other's files, and isolate settings loading so per-agent CLAUDE.md files do not leak across agents.
Container-based sandboxing
Persistent storage: whether the provider offers durable volumes or only ephemeral disk. The hybrid pattern needs durable storage somewhere, whether in the sandbox or alongside it.
Pricing model: per-second, per-request, or flat hourly billing. Per-second pricing suits bursty ephemeral workloads. Hourly suits long-running sessions.
Runtime dependencies
Python 3.10+ for the Python SDK, or Node.js 18.14+ for the TypeScript SDK

Both the TypeScript and Python SDKs bundle a native Claude Code binary for most installs, and the spawned CLI needs no separate Node.js install. See the quickstart's install note for the installs that need a separate native Claude Code install.
Resources
1 GiB RAM, 5 GiB disk, and 1 CPU per agent is a reasonable starting point for a freshly started instance.
Memory usage grows with session length and tool activity, so size for the session lengths and concurrency you actually need rather than the idle baseline.
Scaling and concurrency
Measure the per-session ceiling by running a representative session to your target length under your expected tool load and recording peak RSS.
The 1 GiB starting point in Resources is a floor, not the ceiling.
Cost
Anthropic token cost typically dominates container infrastructure cost by an order of magnitude or more.
A minimally provisioned container runs roughly $0.05 per hour, while a single long agent session can spend dollars in tokens.

pts: Observability with OpenTelemetry

The Agent SDK can export this data as OpenTelemetry traces, metrics, and log events to any backend that accepts the OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP), whether a hosted observability platform or a self-hosted collector.
To read token usage and cost directly from the SDK response stream instead of exporting to a backend, see Track cost and usage.
How telemetry flows from the SDK

Process environment: set the variables in your shell, container, or orchestrator before your application starts. Every query() call picks them up automatically with no code change. This is the recommended approach for production deployments.

Per-call options: set the variables in ClaudeAgentOptions.env (Python) or options.env (TypeScript). Use this when different agents in the same process need different telemetry settings. In Python, env is merged on top of the inherited environment.…
Enable telemetry export
Telemetry is off until you set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and choose at least one exporter.

Because the child process inherits your application's environment by default, you can achieve the same result by exporting these variables in a Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifest, or shell profile and omitting options.env entirely.
Flush telemetry from short-lived calls
On a clean process exit it attempts to flush pending data, but the flush is bounded by a short timeout, so spans can still be dropped if the collector is slow to respond.
By default, metrics export every 60 seconds and traces and logs export every 5 seconds.
Read agent traces
claude_code.interaction: wraps a single turn of the agent loop, from receiving a prompt to producing a response.
claude_code.hook: wraps each hook execution. Requires detailed beta tracing (ENABLE_BETA_TRACING_DETAILED=1 and BETA_TRACING_ENDPOINT), a pair that also changes where your logs and traces go.
Link traces to your application
The SDK automatically propagates W3C trace context into the CLI subprocess.
The agent run then appears inside your application's trace instead of as a disconnected root.
Control sensitive data in exports
The content your agent reads and writes is not recorded by default.
Set to 1 for inline bodies truncated at 60 KB by default, or file: for untruncated bodies on disk with a body_ref path in the event.

notes.w: Isolation and least privilege for agents you ship.
notes.lead: Claude Code and the Agent SDK can execute code, access files, and interact with external services on your behalf.
pts: Securely deploying AI agents
Unlike traditional software that follows predetermined code paths, these tools generate their actions dynamically based on context and goals.
This flexibility is what makes them useful, but it also means their behavior can be influenced by the content they process: files, webpages, or user input.
Sandbox runtime
Filesystem: Uses OS primitives (bubblewrap on Linux, sandbox-exec on macOS) to restrict read/write access to configured paths
Credentials for allowed domains: If the agent has permissive credentials for an allowed domain, ensure it cannot use that domain to trigger other network requests or to exfiltrate data.
Virtual machines
VMs provide hardware-level isolation through CPU virtualization extensions.
It can boot VMs in under 125ms with less than 5 MiB memory overhead, stripping away unnecessary device emulation to reduce attack surface.
Cloud deployments
Run agent containers in a private subnet with no internet gateway 2.
Configure cloud firewall rules (AWS Security Groups, GCP VPC firewall) to block all egress except to your proxy 3.
The proxy pattern
The agent never sees the actual credentials 2.
The proxy can enforce an allowlist of permitted endpoints 3.

This tells Claude Code and the Agent SDK to send sampling requests to your proxy instead of the Claude API directly.
Traffic forwarding
Even if you route it through a proxy via HTTP_PROXY, the proxy only sees an opaque TLS tunnel and can't inject credentials.
For example, Node.js fetch() ignores these variables by default; in Node 24+ you can set NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 to enable support.

Claude built something different from what you had in mind, or it has to rediscover the same fact at the start of every session. It's missing information it can't get from reading the repo. See Tell Claude what it can't see.
Claude did something that must never happen in this repo, or skipped a step that must always happen. A prompt alone can't guarantee either of those. See Enforce the rules that can't have exceptions.
Brainstorm with Claude first
When you don't know exactly what you want yet, you don't have to work it all out before you prompt.
Claude comes back with multiple-choice questions about the parts you haven't pinned down: per-user versus per-key limits, what happens to requests over the limit, what's out of scope.
Keep CLAUDE.md short
Places where the code is misleading: an old pattern that's everywhere but that new code must not copy, or a directory that looks unused but isn't
Decisions that aren't in the repo: which error helper the team settled on, how deploys work, what needs a migration review
Put team procedures in skills
For a skill Claude can start on its own, it sees the name and description in every session, but only reads the full file when the task calls for it.
Claude then can't start the skill on its own, and it only runs when you type /release yourself.
Change the model and effort
When only the next message needs it, like one tricky question in the middle of otherwise routine work, put ultrathink in that prompt instead of changing the setting.
Claude Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 default to medium, which is plenty for everyday feature work with a clear scope.
Know what subagents cost
The subagents it starts run in the background by default, so your main conversation keeps moving.
Give a custom subagent in .claude/agents/ only tools: Read, Grep, Glob. Now it's a reviewer that can't edit anything, and that limit is enforced by Claude Code rather than requested in a prompt.
Keep cost and context down
With a 1M-token window on most current models and compaction near the top of it, you'll rarely run out of context.
It also flags patterns like long context or frequent cache misses once one of them passes 10% of your usage.

notes.w: Undo what Claude changed.
notes.lead: Claude Code automatically tracks Claude's file edits as you work.
pts: Automatic tracking

Claude Code keeps file snapshots for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session. Discarding an older checkpoint deletes the snapshot files that no remaining checkpoint references, except each file's first snapshot, which the VS Code extension uses…

Claude Code deletes a session's file snapshots in the retention sweep, by default about 30 days after the session last saved one. Rewinding to a checkpoint whose snapshots are gone can fail with No files were restored. To keep snapshots longer, set…
Rewind and summarize
Summarize up to here: compress the conversation before this point into a summary, keeping later messages intact
Never mind: return to the message list without making changes
Rewound messages can return if you exit before your next prompt
To remove the returned messages again, run /rewind in the session and select the same prompt, then Restore conversation.
Before you exit, send Claude a prompt, because Claude Code saves the rewound conversation together with that prompt.
Guide a summary
Summarizing doesn't change files on disk, and the original messages stay in the session transcript, so Claude can still reference the details.
To branch off and try a different approach while preserving the original session intact, use /branch or claude --continue --fork-session instead.
Bash command changes not tracked
Once Claude has edited a file with its file editing tools in your conversation, /rewind undoes changes that Bash commands make to that file afterward.
A file that only Bash commands changed isn't tracked and stays as it is.
External changes not tracked
Checkpointing only tracks files that have been edited within the current session.
Manual changes you make to files outside of Claude Code and edits from other concurrent sessions are normally not captured, unless they happen to modify the same files as the current session.
Symlinked and hard-linked paths not restored
Checkpointing doesn't rewind symlinked or hard-linked files.
For every skip reason and the recovery steps, see the skipped-files entry in the error reference.

notes.w: Add a reviewer to a real pull request.
notes.lead: With Code Review, Claude reviews the pull requests in your GitHub repositories.
pts: Code Review
A review with no findings doesn't mean your code is error-free or secure.
How reviews work
Findings: inline comments on the lines concerned, with a summary in the review body
A check run: named Claude Code Review, with the findings listed in its details. The check run doesn't conclude as a failure.
Review levels
Quick: a lighter pass. The fastest level, at the lowest cost.
Standard: balanced depth, speed, and cost. The default level.
What a review can access
Where it runs: on Anthropic infrastructure, in a managed environment. Reviews don't run in self-hosted environments.

What it reads and writes: inside a review, access to your repository is read-only, and a review doesn't push commits. On the pull request, it posts comments and the check run, resolves its own earlier comment threads, and can react to a comment…
Who controls a review

Who can start one: where reviews run automatically, opening or pushing to a pull request starts a review, except on drafts and forks. After some pushes, Code Review keeps the earlier result instead. A comment command starts one only when it comes…
Which instructions it follows: REVIEW.md from the base or default branch and never from the pull request's own changes.

notes.w: Caps and habits that keep spend predictable.
notes.lead: Claude Code charges by API token consumption.
pts: Manage costs effectively
Per-developer costs vary widely based on model selection, codebase size, and usage patterns such as running multiple instances or automation.
Across enterprise deployments, the average cost is around $13 per developer per active day and $150-250 per developer per month, with costs remaining below $30 per active day for 90% of users.
Plan usage breakdown
Recommendations: suggested changes, one per row. Each row starts with a share of your recent usage, at least 10%, as in 25% Trim ~/code/api/CLAUDE.md · 49k tokens per request.
How to read the share: it tells you how much of your usage the row applies to, not how much the change saves. One request can count toward several rows, so the shares can add up to more than 100%.
When the usage request fails

When the request for your plan limits fails, most often because the usage endpoint is rate limited, /usage shows the last usage bars it loaded on this machine within the past 60 minutes, along with a Showing last-known usage note stating how long…
A message such as rate limited until 3:14am in /usage means Claude Code can't fetch your plan limits again until then, not that your work with Claude is limited.
Analyze your usage patterns
A single run analyzes up to 200 sessions it hasn't seen before and skips very short ones.
Claude Code deletes reports on the same schedule as the rest of your session data: at startup, it removes files older than cleanupPeriodDays, 30 days by default.
Claude Console
You can set a rate limit for this workspace on the Rate limits page in the Claude Console to cap the workspace's share and protect other production workloads.
For per-user reporting, the Console dashboard shows spend and lines accepted per member, and the Claude Code Analytics API returns daily per-user metrics programmatically with an Admin API key.
Offload processing to hooks and skills
Instead of Claude reading a 10,000-line log file to find errors, a hook can grep for ERROR and return only matching lines, reducing context from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds.
When Claude invokes the skill, it gets this context immediately instead of spending tokens reading multiple files to understand the structure.
Adjust extended thinking
Extended thinking is enabled by default because it significantly improves performance on complex planning and reasoning tasks.
You can't turn off thinking on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, or the Fable models, which always use extended thinking.

notes.lead: A development container, or dev container, lets you define an identical, isolated environment that every engineer on your team can run.
pts: Development containers
With Claude Code installed in that container, commands Claude runs execute inside it rather than on the host machine, while edits to your project files appear in your local repository as you work.
Add Claude Code to your dev container
The version tag at the end, such as :1.0, pins the feature's install script, not the Claude Code release.
If pasting does nothing, see OAuth login fails in WSL2, SSH, or containers.
Persist authentication and settings across rebuilds
By default, the container's home directory is discarded on rebuild, so engineers must sign in again each time.
It stores your account details, personal MCP servers, and per-project trust in a separate file outside that directory: ~/.claude.json.
Enforce organization policy
For policy that engineers cannot bypass by editing repository files, deliver managed settings through server-managed settings or your MDM instead.

To pin a specific Claude Code version for reproducible builds, install it from your Dockerfile with npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@X.Y.Z instead of using the feature, and set DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER to 1 in containerEnv.
Restrict network egress
You can limit the container's outbound traffic to only the domains Claude Code needs.
The reference container includes an init-firewall.sh script that limits outbound traffic to the destinations the script allows.
Run without permission prompts
Because the container runs Claude Code as a non-root user and confines command execution to the container, you can pass --dangerously-skip-permissions for unattended operation.
Pair this flag with the network egress restrictions above to limit what a bypassed session can reach.
Try the reference container
The anthropics/claude-code repository includes an example dev container that combines the CLI, the egress firewall, persistent volumes, and a Zsh-based shell.
It is provided as a working example rather than a maintained base image; use it to see how the pieces fit together before applying them to your own configuration.

Write specific @claude requests so Claude needs fewer turns to finish

notes.t: Keep Claude working toward a goal
notes.w: Long tasks with a stated finish line.
notes.lead: The /goal command sets a completion condition and Claude keeps working toward it without you prompting each step.
pts: Compare ways to keep a session running
Three approaches keep the current session running between prompts.
The two are complementary: auto mode removes per-tool prompts, and /goal removes per-turn prompts.
Write an effective condition
A stated check: how Claude should prove it, such as "npm test exits 0" or "git status is clean"
Constraints that matter: anything that must not change on the way there, such as "no other test file is modified"
Run non-interactively
With the default text output, Claude's final response prints when the loop ends, so a goal that runs many turns can look stuck.
Add --output-format stream-json --verbose to emit each message as the loop runs.
How evaluation works
Not yet met: Claude keeps working and takes the reason as guidance for the next turn.

Impossible: the evaluator judged that the condition can never be satisfied. Claude Code clears the goal and records a failed entry in the transcript along with the reason. You don't need to clear it yourself.
Other errors retry or pause the goal

Pause: after a failure that a retry would only repeat, such as an API rate limit, a claude.ai usage limit, or a hook that ended the turn, a notice starting with Goal paused names the cause. If the session is waiting to continue automatically when a…
To turn automatic retries off, set CLAUDE_CODE_GOAL_CHECKIN_MINUTES to 0, which also turns check-ins off.
Background work defers evaluation
Once background work has kept the goal waiting for 30 minutes, a check-in is due.
After the first check-in, Claude Code waits twice as long before each later check-in, up to four times the first interval: with the default, 1 hour after the first check-in, then every 2 hours.

Run a prompt repeatedly with /loop: re-run on a time interval instead of toward a condition
Prompt-based hooks: write your own Stop hook when you need custom evaluation logic

notes.w: The -p flag, output formats and limits.
notes.lead: The Agent SDK gives you the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code.
pts: Basic usage
Claude Code rejects --bg, and rejects --cloud with a task description, with an error naming the conflict; --cloud with a session ID and -p instead queues a message into that cloud session and exits.
Claude Code exits with code 0 on success and a non-zero code when the run fails, so your scripts can branch on the exit status.
Give a long subagent command more time
When a subagent's long command moves to the background at its timeout, a claude -p run can exit with code 0 before the command finishes.
To raise the default timeout above the command's run time, set BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS, for example BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS=300000 claude -p "" for five minutes.
Stop a run with SIGTERM
If you stop a claude -p run with SIGTERM, for example with kill or from a process supervisor, Claude Code exits with code 143.
To have Claude Code continue the interrupted turn on resume instead, set CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN=1.
Pipe data through Claude
With --output-format json, the response payload includes total_cost_usd and a per-model cost breakdown, so scripted callers can track spend without consulting the usage dashboard.
If Claude Code can't read stdin, for example because the process that started it disconnected its end, Claude Code prints a warning to stderr and continues with the prompt from the command line.
Fail CI when a plugin or MCP server doesn't load
When you pass --mcp-config with -p, Claude Code waits for still-pending servers before running the first turn, up to the MCP_TIMEOUT startup timeout, 30 seconds by default.

When you run the command yourself in a terminal, Claude Code also prints a startup warning to stderr, such as Warning: 1 MCP server skipped due to invalid config:, followed by the reason for each skipped entry.
Turn off permission prompts in unattended runs
Permission rules, PermissionRequest hooks, and the permission mode you set still decide every call first; Claude Code denies only the requests that nothing else resolves.
With --permission-prompts none, Claude Code removes the tools that need an answer from a person, such as AskUserQuestion, so Claude can't call them.
Customize the system prompt
In the script, "$1" stands for the first argument you pass on the command line.
Run bash review.sh 123 and the shell replaces "$1" with 123, so the script fetches the diff for PR 123.

notes.w: Every event, input and exit code. Look up PreToolUse and Stop here.
notes.lead: Hooks are user-defined shell commands, HTTP endpoints, MCP tool calls, LLM prompts, or subagents that execute automatically at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle.
pts: How a hook resolves
If the command had been a safer rm variant like rm file.txt, the script would hit exit 0 instead.
Exit code 0 with no output means the hook has no decision to report, so the tool call continues through the normal permission flow.
Exit code 0
Exit 0 means success, and is the intended exit code when you print JSON for structured control.
When your hook exits 0 but prints JSON that can't be parsed or fails schema validation, the action goes ahead unless the hook is one whose failure blocks the action.
Other exit codes
A hook error notice with Failed with non-blocking status code: means your hook didn't exit 0 or 2 and its stdout was plain text or empty.
When you set up a policy hook, watch for this notice on its first run, because a mistyped path in settings.json means the hook never runs.
Block the action when a hook fails
HTTP error: an HTTP hook's connection fails, or the response status isn't 2xx

Invalid output: the JSON output can't be parsed or fails schema validation. For an HTTP hook, a 2xx body that is neither empty nor a JSON object also counts. Plain-text stdout from a command hook isn't a failure
Failed hooks on Windows without Git Bash

The hook exits 1 to warn but must block when it crashes: with "onFailure": "continue", the call goes ahead on exit code 1, warning or crash alike. Add "onFailure": "block" instead, and have the script exit 0 where it warns, so those calls go ahead.…
If the error also says PowerShell started no program, start with the fixes for a command that is only quoted strings, which PowerShell prints instead of running.
UserPromptSubmit
UserPromptSubmit hooks have a default timeout of 30 seconds for command, http, and mcp_tool types, shorter than the 600-second default for those types on most other events.

An Agent SDK callback hook on UserPromptSubmit that reaches its timeout blocks the prompt with a message naming the hook and the timeout, because a callback there can be acting as a policy gate that must not fail open.
MessageDisplay
The default timeout for this event is 10 seconds; if your hook needs more time, set the timeout field in the hook entry.
In non-interactive runs, including Agent SDK queries and claude -p, MessageDisplay runs once per assistant message instead of once per batch of lines.

pts: Auto-approve specific permission prompts
Unlike the exit-code examples above, auto-approval requires your hook to write a JSON decision to stdout.
For a tool that requires user interaction, such as ExitPlanMode, the allow also needs updatedInput, or Claude Code ignores it and still shows the prompt.
Hook output

Exit 0: if you exit 0 from a PreToolUse hook, the tool call still goes through the normal permission flow, because exit 0 doesn't approve it. For UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, SessionStart, and PostModelSwitch hooks, Claude Code adds stdout…

Exit 2: write a reason to stderr. Depending on the event, Claude receives it as feedback so it can adjust, the user sees it, or no message appears, as with ConfigChange and Elicitation. Some events can't be blocked: for SessionStart and others, exit…
Prompt-based hooks

PreToolUse: the tool call is denied; by default the turn ends and the deny reason appears in the chat as a warning line. Set continueOnBlock: true on the hook to instead return the reason to Claude as the tool error, so it can adjust and continue
PostToolUse: by default the turn ends and the reason appears in the chat as a warning line. Set continueOnBlock: true to feed the reason back to Claude and continue the turn instead
Agent-based hooks
When verification requires inspecting files or running commands, use type: "agent" hooks.
Agent hooks use the "ok" / "reason" response format with a longer default timeout of 60 seconds and up to 50 tool-use turns.
Limitations
command, http, mcp_tool: 10 minutes. Claude Code lowers this default to 30 seconds for UserPromptSubmit, PreModelSwitch, and PostModelSwitch hooks, and to 10 seconds for MessageDisplay.
SessionEnd hooks of any type share a 1.5-second budget. If your settings set a longer per-hook timeout, Claude Code raises the budget to match, up to 60 seconds.
Shell profile output before the JSON
Because the hook exited 0, the transcript shows no error either.
The $- variable contains shell flags, and i means interactive.
Check what a hook did

Blocking error: on most events you see the message that came with the block, for example Blocked: rm commands are not allowed. On a few events, such as ConfigChange and Elicitation, you see no message. Exit code 2 covers where the message comes from.

Non-blocking error: a hook error notice with Failed with non-blocking status code: means your hook didn't stop the action. You don't see this notice when a command hook on an event such as Notification fails.

notes.w: The agentic loop and the tools it uses.
notes.lead: Claude Code is an agentic assistant that runs in your terminal.
pts: The agentic loop
A question about your codebase might only need context gathering.
Claude decides what each step requires based on what it learned from the previous step, chaining dozens of actions together and course-correcting along the way.
Models
Claude Code uses Claude models to understand your code and reason about tasks.

The other permission modes change which of these ask you; in auto mode a classifier reviews actions instead of you, and how the classifier evaluates actions lists which ones it sees.

A broad deny rule like Bash(aws *) blocks every matching call, including calls that also match a narrower allow rule like Bash(aws s3 ls).
Bare-name removal applies to every tool except EndConversation: a deny rule can't remove it while any other tool remains, and an ask rule never prompts for it.

Every subcommand must be allowed for a compound command to run without a prompt, for example because the subcommand matches an allow rule or is a read-only command.

Before matching Bash rules, Claude Code strips a fixed set of wrappers, so a rule like Bash(npm test *) also matches timeout 30 npm test.

notes.lead: Prompt caching makes Claude Code faster and more cost-efficient.
pts: How the cache is organized
Model: each model has its own cache. Switching models recomputes the entire request even when the content is identical. See Switching models below.

Effort level: on most models, each effort level has its own cache, so changing effort mid-session recomputes the entire request. With an API key or a Claude subscription, the cache stays intact by default on Fable 5.1 and later, Opus 5.5, Sonnet…
Switching models
Switching with /model means the next request reads the entire conversation history with no cache hits, even though the content is identical.
Automatic model fallback on Fable models, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Opus 5 is also a model switch.
Changing effort level
On most models, changing the effort level mid-session means the next request reads the entire conversation history with no cache hits.
With an API key or a Claude subscription, changing effort keeps the cache on Fable 5.1 and later, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5.
Accumulating many images
When the next request would pass either limit, Claude Code removes a batch of the oldest images and PDFs from what it sends, which leaves room for more before it needs to remove any again.
Because Claude Code removes a batch at a time, you see one slower turn per batch rather than one with each new screenshot.
Choose the TTL yourself

Amazon Bedrock: prompt caching support, minimum cacheable prefix length, and one-hour TTL availability all vary by model. If cache token counts stay at zero, check supported models, regions, and limits in the Amazon Bedrock documentation.
If you sign in with an API key or use a cloud provider, set promptCacheTtl to 1h to give the main conversation a one-hour cache.
Subagents and the cache
Session copies: a session you copy with /fork receives its isolation instruction as a message at the end of the copied conversation, so the cache that the original conversation built stays intact.

Workflow fan-outs: in a workflow fan-out of same-prefix agents, Claude Code holds all but the first for up to 5 seconds by default, so their first requests can read the prefix that the first agent cached.

notes.w: Plain definitions of tokens, context, temperature and the other terms in this course.
notes.lead: These concepts are not unique to Claude. This page presents a brief summary of key terms.
pts: Context window
The “context window” refers to the amount of text a language model can look back on and reference when generating new text.
This is different from the large corpus of data the language model was trained on, and instead represents a “working memory” for the model.
Fine-tuning
Fine-tuning is the process of further training a pretrained language model using additional data.

Fine-tuning can be useful for adapting a language model to a specific domain, task, or writing style, but it requires careful consideration of the fine-tuning data and the potential impact on the model’s performance and biases.
HHH
A helpful AI will attempt to perform the task or answer the question posed to the best of its abilities, providing relevant and useful information.
A harmless AI will not be offensive or discriminatory, and when asked to aid in a dangerous or unethical act, the AI should politely refuse and explain why it cannot comply.
Latency
Latency, in the context of generative AI and large language models, refers to the time it takes for the model to respond to a given prompt.
Lower latency indicates faster response times, which is crucial for real-time applications, chatbots, and interactive experiences.
RAG (retrieval augmented generation)
When generating text, relevant information first must be retrieved from the knowledge base based on the input prompt, and then passed to the model along with the original query.
RAG can be particularly useful for tasks that require up-to-date information, domain-specific knowledge, or explicit citation of sources.
Temperature

Request size limits

notes.w: Per-minute limits, cache-aware input counting, ramp limits and the monthly spend cap.
notes.lead: To mitigate misuse and manage capacity on the API, limits are in place on how much an organization can use the Claude API.
pts: About rate limits

You might hit rate limits over shorter time intervals. For instance, a rate of 60 requests per minute (RPM) might be enforced as 1 request per second. Short bursts of requests can exceed the limit and trigger rate limit errors.
The API uses the token bucket algorithm to do rate limiting. This means that your capacity is continuously replenished up to your maximum limit, rather than being reset at fixed intervals.
Setting your own spend limit
When usage reaches a spend limit you set, requests return HTTP 400 with error type invalid_request_error.
Limits on the Claude Code workspace are checked separately: Claude Code requests over that workspace’s limit can instead receive a 429 that carries a retry-after header.
Rate limits
The rate limits for the Messages API are measured in requests per minute (RPM), input tokens per minute (ITPM), and output tokens per minute (OTPM) for each model class.
If you exceed any of the rate limits, you get a 429 error describing which rate limit was exceeded.
Cache-aware ITPM
The API’s default ITPM rate limits count only uncached input tokens.

Example: With a 2,000,000 ITPM limit and an 80 percent cache hit rate, you could effectively process 10,000,000 total input tokens per minute (2M uncached + 8M cached), because cached tokens don’t count toward your rate limit.
Ramp limits
The step and the starting amount vary by model and can change. The error message usually states your current ramp limit, the step, and your rate limit.
The error type is rate_limit_error, the same as for a rate limit. On the Messages API, error.details.error_code is ramp_limit_exceeded. Use it to tell this response apart from a rate limit.
Fast mode rate limits
Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Mythos 5.2, and Claude Opus 5.5 have a default fast mode rate limit.
When you exceed your fast mode rate limits, the API returns a 429 error with a retry-after header.
Setting lower limits for workspaces
On Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) and Claude Platform on AWS, you can’t set spend limits on the default workspace.
Example: If your organization’s limit is 40,000 input tokens per minute and 8,000 output tokens per minute, you might limit one workspace to 30,000 input tokens per minute.

pts: How cache diagnostics works
For each request that includes the diagnostics object, the API stores a lightweight fingerprint keyed by the response id.

Fingerprints contain only hashes and token-count estimates (never raw prompt content), are retained for a limited time, are scoped to your organization and workspace, and are not used for any other purpose.
Basic usage
The object is the opt-in: the API stores a fingerprint only for requests that include it.
On the first turn, pass "previous_message_id": null to opt in without a prior message to compare against.
Streaming
In streaming responses, diagnostics appears on the message_start event.
The message_start event carries the full diagnostics field; see Response format for the possible values.
Cache miss reason types
The response reports the earliest divergence only, so fix it first; later ones might be hidden behind it.

The four *_changed types also carry a cache_missed_input_tokens integer: an estimate of how many input tokens fell after the divergence point, giving you a sense of how much cacheable prefix was lost.
Reading diagnostics alongside usage
diagnostics tells you whether your request changed, and usage.cache_read_input_tokens tells you whether the cache hit.
On the first turn (previous_message_id: null), diagnostics is always null and cache_read_input_tokens is normally zero because the cache is being written, not read; no troubleshooting is needed.
Limitations
Comparison horizon: For very long conversations where the only change is deep in the message list, the response might be unavailable rather than a precise location.

Best-effort: Diagnostics never blocks or fails your request. If diagnostic information is not available, the response returns unavailable, or cache_miss_reason: null when the comparison was still running.
Data retention
The API stores a fingerprint only for requests that include the diagnostics object.
The fingerprint consists only of cryptographic hashes and token-count estimates, keyed by the response id and scoped to your organization and workspace.

notes.w: What the window holds, and why a bigger window is not perfect recall.
notes.lead: Understand how the context window works, how extended thinking and tool use count toward it, and how to manage context as conversations grow.
pts: How the context window works

Progressive token accumulation: As the conversation advances through turns, each user message and assistant response accumulates within the context window, and previous turns are preserved completely.
Context window capacity: The context window (up to 1M tokens, depending on the model) holds the conversation history plus the new output Claude generates.
Context window sizes by model
A single request to any of them can generate up to 128k output tokens (max_tokens).

For every model with a 1M-token context window, 1M is the default: you don’t need a beta header, and long-context requests are billed at standard pricing, except on Claude Haiku 5.5, where prompts over 100,000 tokens cost more.
The context window with thinking
Claude Sonnet 4.6 and later Sonnet models
Claude Mythos 5.2, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Mythos 5, and Claude Mythos Preview
The context window with thinking and tool use
Output components: After tool results have been passed back to Claude, Claude responds with only text (no additional thinking until the next user message, unless interleaved thinking is enabled).

It is automatic on models with adaptive thinking; Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5 (deprecated), and earlier Claude 4 models require the interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14 beta header, and Claude Haiku 4.5 does not support it.
Context awareness

Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.5 (deprecated), and Claude Haiku 4.5 have context awareness: these models track their remaining context window (their “token budget”) throughout a conversation.
Context awareness is automatic: there is nothing for you to enable, and you never send the tags shown in this section yourself.
How it works
The budget matches the context window available to your request: 1M tokens for Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, and 200k tokens for Claude Sonnet 4.5 (deprecated) and Claude Haiku 4.5.
The examples in this section show a model with a 200k-token context window.
Context window overflow behavior
If the input alone already exceeds the model’s context window, the API returns a 400 invalid_request_error (“prompt is too long”) on every model.
On Claude 4.5 models and newer, if input tokens plus max_tokens exceeds the context window size, the API accepts the request.

pts: How effort works
Most Claude models default to high effort, spending as many tokens as needed for excellent results; Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 default to medium.
Setting effort to the model’s default ("medium" on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, "high" on other models) produces exactly the same behavior as omitting the effort parameter entirely.
Effort levels
At lower effort levels, Claude still thinks on sufficiently difficult problems, but thinks less than it would at higher effort levels for the same problem.
The per-model recommendations that follow override this table where they differ.
Recommended effort levels
Medium effort: Cost-saving step-down from the default. Comparable to Claude Sonnet 4.6 at high effort.
With between_tools, effort can’t change mid-conversation: a per-message output_config.effort at a different level returns a 400 error.
Effort with thinking

On Claude Opus 4.5, the only extended-thinking-only model that supports effort, it works alongside budget_tokens: set the effort level for your task, then set the thinking token budget based on how much reasoning depth the task needs.
For per-model thinking availability, see the per-model configuration table.
Change effort mid-conversation
You can run later turns of a conversation at a different effort level in two ways.
A per-message effort change keeps the prompt cache.
Top-level effort on the next request
Because top-level effort shapes the rendered prompt, changing it between requests can invalidate cached prefixes from earlier turns.
If you rely on prompt caching across a long session and your model doesn’t support per-message effort, pick an effort level at the start and keep it constant.
Best practices
Set effort explicitly: The API defaults to high (medium on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5), but the right starting point depends on your model and workload.
On models that support it, use a per-message effort change instead, which preserves the cache.

Up to 2.5x higher output tokens per second compared to standard speed

Falling back to standard speed

notes.w: Breakpoints, lifetime and the usage fields that prove a hit.
notes.lead: Cache prompt prefixes with cache_control to cut costs and latency, using automatic caching or explicit breakpoints with 5-minute or 1-hour TTLs.
pts: How prompt caching works
By default, the cache has a 5-minute lifetime.

Time spent generating a response counts against the lifetime: if a response takes 4 minutes to stream, a follow-up request that reuses the same cached prefix must start within about 1 minute of that response completing.
Pricing
Cache write tokens with a 5-minute TTL are 1.25 times the base input tokens price.
Cache read tokens are 0.1 times the base input tokens price (see the table footnote for per-model exceptions).
Edge cases
If the last block has an explicit cache_control with a different TTL, the API returns a 400 error.
If 4 explicit block-level breakpoints already exist, the API returns a 400 error (no slots left for automatic caching).
Understanding cache breakpoint costs
Cache writes: When new content is written to the cache (25 percent more than base input tokens for 5-minute TTL)
Cache reads: When cached content is used (10 percent of base input token price, with per-model exceptions)
Cache limitations

To check whether a prompt was cached, look at the response usage fields: if both cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are 0, the prompt was not cached (likely because it did not meet the minimum length requirement).
ephemeral is the only supported cache type, which by default has a 5-minute lifetime.
Cache storage and sharing
Organization isolation: Different organizations never share caches, even if they use identical prompts.
Exact matching: Cache hits require 100 percent identical prompt segments, including all text and images up to and including the block marked with cache control.
Typical usage pattern

notes.lead: Comprehensive guide to prompt engineering techniques for Claude's latest models, covering clarity, examples, XML structuring, thinking, and agentic systems.
pts: Long context prompting
Put long-form data at the top: Place your long documents and inputs near the top of your prompt, above your query, instructions, and examples. This improves performance across all models.
Queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests, especially with complex, multidocument inputs.
Communication style and verbosity
Claude Opus 5 is an exception on verbosity: its default user-facing responses run longer than prior models’, and raising or lowering effort does not reliably change visible response length.
Claude Fable 5.1 has the opposite tendency during agentic work: it writes fewer user-facing updates between tool calls.
Control the format of responses
Try: “Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs.”
Claude Fable 5.1 already formats less than earlier models, so on that model a block like this can suppress structure the content needs.
Migrating away from prefilled responses
Starting with Claude 4.6 models and Claude Mythos Preview, prefilled responses (providing a partial assistant message for Claude to continue from) on the last assistant turn are no longer supported.
Requests with prefilled assistant messages to these models return a 400 error.
Overthinking and excessive thoroughness
If you need a hard ceiling on thinking costs, extended thinking with a budget_tokens cap is still functional on Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 but is deprecated.
On Claude 4.7 and later models, setting budget_tokens returns a 400 error.
Leverage thinking and interleaved thinking capabilities
On Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Mythos 5.2, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Fable 5, Claude Mythos 5, and Claude Opus 5.5, thinking is always on and adaptive thinking is the only mode.
On Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Haiku 5.5, thinking is on by default when you omit the thinking parameter, so a response can begin with thinking blocks.
Migration considerations
On Claude 4.7 and later models, setting budget_tokens returns a 400 error.
Migrate away from prefilled responses: Prefilled responses on the last assistant turn are no longer supported starting with Claude 4.6 models and Claude Mythos Preview.

notes.lead: Prompting patterns specific to Claude Haiku 5.5: effort, search, JSON output with your own tools, early stopping, coding verification, mid-turn user messages, system prompt adherence in chatbots, reasoning in user-facing text, and refusals.
pts: Use effort to control thinking

Thinking is on by default and counts toward max_tokens, which can go up to 128,000. A max_tokens value sized for Claude Haiku 4.5 requests that ran without thinking can cut the reply off, so leave room for thinking.

Changing the top-level output_config.effort value between requests invalidates the prompt cache for the conversation’s messages. On supported platforms, you can change the level partway through a conversation with a per-message effort change, which…
Accurate search results
When you give Claude Haiku 5.5 a search tool, also give it today’s date.
On prompts that need no search, it added searches in only 0–3 percent of tries.
Use adaptive thinking with JSON output and your own tools
With thinking off, Claude Haiku 5.5 might skip a tool call it needs when you also request JSON output with structured outputs.
Remove output_config.format from any request where the model must call a tool.
Prevent early stopping in long agent prompts
With a short system prompt, Claude Haiku 5.5 rarely stops before the work is done.
With a long coding-agent system prompt at low effort, it sometimes stops early and hands the task back to the user.
Tell coding agents to verify their changes
At low and medium effort, Claude Haiku 5.5 sometimes reports a code change as done without running a check.
In Anthropic’s testing, the model checked its changes more often with this text, and its performance improved, at the cost of more tokens.
Mid-turn user messages
Keep harness notices, such as reminders, in a separate mid-conversation system message. Never put a notice and the user’s words in the same block.
Claude Haiku 5.5 is trained to resist prompt injection through tool results.
Safeguard refusals
Claude Haiku 5.5 runs safety classifiers that can decline a request.
Code written for Claude Haiku 4.5 might not handle these refusals.

notes.w: Model-specific advice. Each model likes slightly different prompts.

pts: Steer initiative and scope
How far Claude Sonnet 5.5 goes on its own depends on the effort level and the request.
When a request is open-ended, for example “show me what you can do with this,” the model can start building a presentation, report, or video when you only wanted ideas.
Running without up-front thinking

Send between_tools at high effort or below. At xhigh or max effort, a request with between_tools returns a 400 error. With between_tools, effort also can’t change mid-conversation: a per-message output_config.effort that differs from the level in…

Use adaptive thinking for reasoning tasks without tools. In a request without tools, between_tools means the model answers without thinking first. For tasks that need a few steps of working out, use adaptive thinking instead. See Reasoning tasks…
Reasoning tasks with JSON output

Also consider xhigh effort with adaptive thinking. The model then works the problem out in its thinking and nearly always returns the JSON alone. Total output tokens stay about the same as at high, because the working moves from the response text…
With structured outputs, the response text holds only the JSON, so the model can work the problem out only in its thinking.
User-facing progress updates
Between tool calls, Claude Sonnet 5.5 writes user-facing notes about what it just found and what it’s doing next.

With between_tools, the notes come back with their summary text, so no display field is needed. between_tools takes no other field: display, budget_tokens, or block_binding sent with it returns a 400 error.
Tool use in chat and knowledge work
On chat and knowledge-work tasks, Claude Sonnet 5.5 sometimes answers from its training knowledge when a web search would catch details that have changed.
First, check your prompt for language that discourages tool use, such as “only use tools when strictly necessary” or “minimize tool calls,” and remove it.
Verification on coding tasks
On agentic coding tasks, Claude Sonnet 5.5 generally checks its work before it reports a change as done.
For example, it might skip the project’s tests because the project’s dependencies aren’t installed.
Safeguard refusals
Claude Sonnet 5.5 runs safety classifiers that can decline a request.
If you turn on server-side fallback (in beta), it retries cyber and frontier_llm declines on Claude Sonnet 5.

notes.w: Cap what a long task may spend.
notes.lead: Give Claude an advisory token budget for the full agentic loop to help the model self-regulate on long agentic tasks.
pts: When to use task budgets
You want Claude to self-regulate token spend on long-horizon tasks.
You have a predictable per-task cost or latency ceiling to enforce.
How the budget countdown works
Claude receives a budget-countdown marker injected server-side throughout the conversation.

If you also decrement remaining while resending full history, the model receives an under-reported budget and the countdown drops faster than it should, causing Claude to finish earlier than the budget actually allows.
What counts as a turn
The budget covers one agentic turn, also called an agentic loop: everything Claude does in response to one user message that carries no tool results.
Today, that exclusion applies only to the budget carried across a server-side compaction; earlier turns’ history still counts while it remains in the context.
Worked example: budget counting across requests
Suppose this assistant message (thinking plus the tool call) totals 5,000 generated tokens.
The countdown Claude received during generation ended near remaining ≈ 95,000.
Carrying a budget across compaction with remaining
Leave out anything still present in the messages you send, including any summary you added, because the server counts those tokens itself.
Update this figure only when you replace the history this way; don’t decrement it on each request.
Task budgets are advisory, not enforced
Use max_tokens as the absolute ceiling that prevents runaway generation.

When Claude receives a budget that is clearly insufficient for the work being asked (for example, a 20,000-token budget for a multihour agentic coding task), it might decline to attempt the task at all, scope it down aggressively, or stop early with…
Measure your current usage
Start with the p99 of your per-task token spend to understand how providing the model with a task budget might modify the model’s behavior, then test up or down as needed.
The minimum accepted task_budget.total is 20,000 tokens on every model that supports task budgets (see Feature support).

pts: Configuring thinking

Turning thinking off
A per-message output_config.effort that differs from the level in effect also returns a 400 error while thinking is off.
And if any thinking configuration comes back with a 400 error, Troubleshooting thinking matches each error message to its fix.
Controlling thinking display

display is invalid with thinking.type: "disabled" (there is nothing to display) and with thinking.type: "between_tools" (Claude Sonnet 5.5 only), which accepts no other field. With between_tools, progress updates still come back with summary text…

The primary benefit is faster time-to-first-text-token when streaming: the server skips streaming thinking tokens entirely and delivers only the signature, so the final text response starts streaming sooner.
Thinking and effort
You need a hard ceiling on spend: use max_tokens. Effort is soft guidance. max_tokens is a strict limit.
On Claude Opus 4.5, the only extended-thinking-only model that supports effort, effort composes with budget_tokens.
Preserving thinking blocks
To override the default, use the clear_thinking_20251015 context-editing strategy.
Within the latest assistant message, the sequence of consecutive thinking blocks must match what the model generated in the original request: you can’t rearrange, edit, or partially drop them.
Response prefill and forced tool use
Claude 4.6 and later models and Claude Mythos Preview reject a prefilled final assistant turn with a 400 error, whether or not thinking is on (see Prefill not supported).
The exceptions are Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Mythos 5.2, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Mythos 5.1, which reject forced tool use on every request with a 400 error.
Long requests
The SDK requires streaming when max_tokens is greater than 21,333, to avoid HTTP timeouts on long-running requests.

For workloads that push thinking above roughly 32k tokens per request, use batch processing to avoid networking issues: such requests can run long enough to hit system timeouts and open connection limits.

The temperature, top_p, and top_k sampling parameters are not supported on Claude 4.7 and later models and Claude Mythos Preview, or on any model starting with API version 2026-10-21.
Setting them to a non-default value returns a 400 error, and starting with 2026-10-21 any value does.
Multiple conversational turns
The Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API.
A thread expires 5 minutes after its last request and is deleted no more than 1 hour after its last use.
System role in messages

A mid-conversation system message has the same authority as the top-level system field, but because it is appended to the end of the message history, it does not invalidate any cached prefix that came before it.
Use the top-level system field for instructions that should apply from the very first turn, and a mid-conversation system message for instructions that only become relevant later.
Prefilling Claude’s response

Claude 4.5 and earlier models: The API accepts a prefill unless the model is retired on the platform that you use. All requests to a retired model fail. To check a model’s status, see Model deprecations.
All other models: The API returns a 400 error (see the Prefill not supported section of the Claude API errors page). Use one of the alternatives to a prefill instead.

JSON that follows a schema: Use structured outputs, which constrain the response to follow the schema.
Another output format: Describe the format in the system prompt, which is the request’s system field.

Time buckets are optional: Set time_bucket_width to 1m, 1h, or 1d to split each combination by UTC bucket; each row’s starting_at and ending_at are then its bucket’s bounds. Buckets with no usage or cost produce no rows.

Ranked by default: Rows are ordered by the order_by metric across the whole range, largest first by default (order=asc reverses it). To build a time series, set time_bucket_width and order_by=time. Rows then come back one time bucket after another…
Usage endpoint
GET /v1/organizations/analytics/usage returns token counts by type. order_by accepts total_tokens (the default), output_tokens, uncached_input_tokens, requests, or time.
To look up API key and workspace IDs, use the List API Keys and List Workspaces endpoints or the Claude Console.

pts: Define your success criteria
Specific: Clearly define what you want to achieve. Instead of “good performance,” specify “accurate sentiment classification.”
Likert scales: “Rate coherence from 1 (nonsensical) to 5 (perfectly logical)”
Common success criteria
You might also need to consider edge case handling, such as how well the model needs to perform on rare or challenging inputs.
Most use cases need multidimensional evaluation along several success criteria.
Eval design principles
Ambiguous test cases where even humans would find it hard to reach an assessment consensus
Be task-specific: Design evals that mirror your real-world task distribution.
Example evals
Example eval test cases: 1,000 tweets with human-labeled sentiments.
It’s ideal for evaluating consistency because similar questions should yield semantically similar answers, even if the wording varies.
Grade your evaluations
Code-based grading: Fastest and most reliable, extremely scalable, but also lacks nuance for more complex judgments that require less rule-based rigidity.
Human grading: Most flexible and high quality, but slow and expensive.
Tips for LLM-based grading
Have detailed, clear rubrics: “The answer should always mention ‘Acme Inc.’ in the first sentence. If it does not, the answer is automatically graded as ‘incorrect.’”

Be empirical or specific: For example, instruct the LLM to output only ‘correct’ or ‘incorrect’, or to judge from a scale of 1–5. Purely qualitative evaluations are hard to assess quickly and at scale.

notes.w: Screens and checks to add to your eval.
notes.lead: Defend your application against jailbreaks and prompt injection with input screening, hardened system prompts, and safe handling of untrusted tool content.
pts: Jailbreaks and direct prompt injection

Harmlessness screens: Use a lightweight model such as Claude Haiku 5.5 to pre-screen user input before it reaches your main conversation. Use structured outputs to constrain the response to a simple classification. Claude Haiku 5.5 runs safety…

Input validation: Filter user input for known injection patterns before it reaches Claude. You can use an LLM to create a generalized validation screen by providing known jailbreaking language as examples.
Indirect prompt injection

State the policy in your system prompt. Tell Claude explicitly that content returned from tools, documents, or searches is untrusted data and must never override the system prompt or the user’s original request.

Screen tool outputs before Claude acts on them. Apply the same lightweight-model screening pattern you use for user input to the content your tools return. Run each tool, pass its raw output to a small classifier call with Claude Haiku 5.5, and only…
Continuous monitoring
Regularly analyze outputs for signs of successful injection.
Use this monitoring to iteratively refine your prompts, validation, and filtering strategies.
Advanced: Chain safeguards
Use structured outputs to constrain the response to a boolean classification.

By layering these strategies, you create a robust defense against jailbreaking and prompt injections, ensuring your Claude-powered applications maintain the highest standards of safety and compliance.

notes.w: Anthropic's own checklist for making invented answers less likely. Use it on your failure log.
notes.lead: Minimize hallucinations in Claude's outputs by allowing uncertainty, grounding responses in direct quotes, and verifying claims with citations.
pts: Basic hallucination minimization strategies
Allow Claude to say “I don’t know”: Explicitly give Claude permission to admit uncertainty. This technique can drastically reduce false information.

Verify with citations: Make Claude’s response auditable by having it cite quotes and sources for each of its claims. You can also have Claude verify each claim by finding a supporting quote after it generates a response. If it can’t find a quote, it…
Advanced techniques
Best-of-N verification: Run Claude through the same prompt multiple times and compare the outputs. Inconsistencies across outputs could indicate hallucinations.
External knowledge restriction: Explicitly instruct Claude to only use information from provided documents and not its general knowledge.

notes.w: Levers for speed, in order of effort.
notes.lead: Reduce Claude's response latency by choosing a faster model such as Claude Haiku 5.5, trimming prompt and output tokens, and streaming responses.
pts: How to measure latency

Baseline latency: This is the time taken by the model to process the prompt and generate the response, without considering the input and output tokens per second. It provides a general idea of the model’s speed.

Time to first token (TTFT): This metric measures the time it takes for the model to generate the first token of the response, from when the prompt was sent. It’s particularly relevant when you’re using streaming (more on that later) and want to…
1. Choose the right model
Consider your specific requirements and choose the model that best fits your needs in terms of speed and output quality.
For speed-critical applications, Claude Haiku 5.5 offers the fastest response times while maintaining high intelligence.
2. Optimize prompt and output length
Set appropriate output limits: Use the max_tokens parameter to set a hard limit on the maximum length of the generated response. This prevents Claude from generating overly long outputs.
instead of words, asking for an exact word count or a word count limit is not as effective a strategy as asking for paragraph or sentence count limits.
3. Stream responses
Streaming is a feature that allows the model to start sending back its response before the full output is complete.
This can significantly improve the perceived responsiveness of your application, as users can see the model’s output in real time.

notes.t: When to use web search, extended thinking and research
notes.w: Three switches that are easy to confuse.
notes.lead: Claude offers several powerful capabilities to help you find information and solve problems.
pts: When should I use web search, extended thinking, and research?
Understanding when to use each option—web search, extended thinking, and research—can help you get the best results for your specific needs.
Web search

Web search is best for straightforward, factual queries that can be answered with one or two tool calls, such as checking the weather, getting info about a specific company, retrieving recent news headlines, or getting up-to-date details like "who…
It's also helpful if you want to steer Claude more—you want to tell it generally what to search, but also want it to handle the process of actually running the web searches and analyzing the results.
Extended thinking

Extended thinking shines when tackling complex reasoning tasks that don't require recent info from the web—like solving mathematical problems, debugging code, or analyzing philosophical concepts—allowing Claude to explore multiple angles before…
Extended thinking on its own is best if you don't want to search the web or use integrations, but just want Claude to think harder about your query to figure out the answer.
Research

Research is optimal for comprehensive information gathering requiring five or more tool calls over 1-3 minutes, creating in-depth reports by synthesizing information from multiple sources across the web and your integrations.
It can do things like compare business competitors, update outdated internal documents with info from the web, help you prioritize or action items from your calendar and email, and more.
Use research and extended thinking together
The research feature can synthesize information across multiple sources with proper citations and produces a longer final report.

Custom skills
